candidate_targets: people using conditional achievements to validate self-worth
contraindications: May not be suitable for individuals with severe depression or psychosis where negative self-judgments are pervasive and not easily observed; may increase distress if not supported properly.
original_extraction.evidence_text:
Now, in trying to raise your self-esteem, you gather as many white pieces together as you can with
thoughts like, ‘My boss just gave me a pay rise’, ‘I’m going to the gym three times a week’, ‘I’m
helping my best friend though a major crisis’, and so on.

---

As you advance these white pieces across the board, your self-esteem starts to rise. But here’s the
problem: there’s a whole army of black pieces waiting to counterattack! And the moment you slip
up—the moment you stop doing any of those things you’re using to justify ‘I’m a good person’—
those black pieces attack and your self-esteem dissolves like a sugar cube in the rain.

---

You stop exercising for a few days and you get, ‘See? You knew it couldn’t last! You’re so
pathetic!’ You lose your temper with a friend and you get, ‘What sort of lousy friend are you?’ You
make a mistake at work and you get, ‘Jeez, what a loser—you can’t even do your job right!’

---

So then you need to rally some more white pieces. Some people try to do this with positive
affirmations, repeating over and over things like, ‘I love, cherish and approve of myself”, ‘I am a
wonderful human being, full of love, strength and courage.’ The problem with such affirmations is
that most people don’t really believe what they are saying. It’s a bit like saying, ‘I am Superman’,
or “I am Wonder Woman.” No matter how often you said that to yourself, you wouldn’t really
believe it, would you?

---

Another problem is that any positive affirmation you use, regardless of whether it’s ‘true’, naturally
tends to attract a negative response. (The white pieces always attract the black pieces.) To illustrate
this, try the following exercise.

---

In this exercise, read each sentence slowly and try your very hardest to believe it. As you do so,
notice what your thinking self does in reaction; that is, notice what thoughts automatically pop into
your head.

---

«Jam a worthwhile, lovable, valuable human being.
generation_rules: Use metaphor of a board game with white and black pieces to represent positive and negative self-evaluations
Present examples of positive achievements followed by negative self-judgments
Introduce exercises that encourage noticing automatic negative thoughts in response to positive affirmations
pause_rules: Pause after presenting positive affirmations to allow the individual to notice automatic negative thoughts.
original_extraction.psychological_function: To reveal the automatic negative thoughts that counteract attempts to boost self-esteem through achievements or positive affirmations, highlighting the conflict between self-justifying thoughts and self-critical responses.
repetition_rules: Repeat examples of positive achievements followed by negative self-judgments to emphasize the pattern of self-esteem fluctuation.
symbolic_elements: white pieces representing positive achievements or self-justifications
black pieces representing negative self-judgments or counterattacks
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: To illustrate the instability of self-esteem based on conditional achievements and to expose the automatic negative self-judgments that undermine positive self-views.
voice_rules: Use a conversational and illustrative tone
Encourage self-observation and awareness of internal reactions
